questions.title: Liver surgery when extrahepatic disease is present or treated
questions.question: Does present or previously treated extrahepatic disease preclude liver cytoreduction or resection for well-differentiated NET liver metastases?
questions.proposal: Extrahepatic disease does not by itself preclude hepatic cytoreduction or resection of the primary for well-differentiated G1–G2 disease when at least 70% of liver disease can be removed or treated and accessible extrahepatic disease can be resected at the same time. Frame it as life-prolonging debulking; extrahepatic disease is associated with shorter survival in most, but not all, series (NANETS describes the data as conflicting).
rules: Proceed when ≥70% debulking is achievable and accessible extrahepatic disease (mesenteric nodes, limited peritoneal deposits) can be removed; resect distant nodes only when this renders the patient free of visible disease.
Bone metastases are an adverse modifier, not an automatic exclusion; diffuse skeletal, brain or unresectable mesenteric-root disease argue against surgery.
No observation period is required before cytoreduction.
Transplant questions go to NET-B4.
questions.rationale: NANETS consensus accepts extrahepatic disease for cytoreduction; cohorts show it shortens survival.

studies.population: NANETS small-bowel NET consensus. Recommendation 5d: extrahepatic disease is not an absolute contraindication to cytoreduction; 5c: patients with extrahepatic disease may be eligible for liver debulking when ≥70% debulking is achievable.
studies.results: Distant nodes resected only in select cases (threatening vital structures, or to achieve no evidence of disease).
studies.limits: Expert consensus.

positions.says: Retrospective 123-patient series: bland embolisation outperformed chemoembolisation on response in carcinoid (81.0% vs 44.4%) without survival difference; islet-cell results trended the other way. Roadmap critique: the referring physician chose technique, so effects are confounded.

questions.divergence: NCCN accepts both techniques while ENETS 2024 leans to bland embolisation in small-intestine NET and ENETS 2023 to chemoembolisation in functioning pancreatic NET, and the comparative data are either underpowered or confounded by referral.
questions.proposal: No default is set. Bland embolisation and conventional TACE are both Reasonable (grade C), chosen by burden, symptoms, liver reserve and biliary-infection risk and not treated as interchangeable; drug-eluting embolics are avoided. The roadmap calls the default an expertise-and-availability decision, with technique, goal, hepatic progression-free survival and toxicity recorded for every procedure.

questions.rationale: The only prospective three-way comparison is still enrolling and its drug-eluting-bead arm closed for severe complications. One small randomised TAE versus TACE trial (Maire 2012, 26 patients, cited from ENETS rather than read in full) found no significant 2-year progression-free survival difference but was underpowered. The best non-randomised comparison favours bland embolisation on response in carcinoid disease (81.0% versus 44.4%, odds ratio 6.41) with no survival difference, but treatment was chosen by the referring physician; ENETS 2024 prefers bland in small-intestine NET while ENETS 2023 calls chemoembolisation possibly more effective in functioning pancreatic NET. Any choice is expertise and availability.
questions.audit: Registry: technique, goal, hepatic progression-free survival, toxicity.

questions.divergence: Targets run from more than 90% (NCCN) through 70% (NANETS 2017) and 70–90% (ENETS 2023) to none at all (ENETS 2024, ESMO), and no comparative study supports any of them.
questions.proposal: No percentage is adopted as evidence. Operate only when a named target can be cleared, with the expected residual stated beforehand, in a patient fit for a long operation with enough functional parenchyma; avoid diffuse-miliary disease and liver replacement above roughly 50–70%. The open NELM-R1 proposal uses at least 70% achievable debulking when extrahepatic disease is present.

questions.rationale: Debulking series are single-arm and selection-driven and no threshold is evidence-derived. The 90% figure was an observation about symptom relief, never validated oncologically; the 70% figure was set by consensus on two retrospective series from the championing centres, and the cohort most cited for it excluded by design every patient in whom 70% was unachievable, so it has no sub-70% arm. NANETS 2020 reached no consensus for pancreatic primaries.
questions.audit: Registry: burden before and after, residual, liver progression-free survival.

NCCN still calls transplantation investigational and NELM is a nonstandard exception, not a standardised one. Graft stewardship is an institutional judgement.

questions.title: Does transplantation offer enough additional benefit?
questions.question: Which patients gain enough over modern non-LT treatment?
questions.context: Establish what additional benefit transplantation offers over available treatment or surveillance.

positions.says: “expert-driven and hypothesis-generating framework (not outcome-validated)” Illustrative survival figures are discussion aids, not calibrated individual eligibility thresholds.
positions.locator: 2026 full-text PDF p3, transplant-benefit discussion

questions.proposal: Require a demonstrable benefit trigger; excellent predicted post-LT survival alone is not enough.
rules: Proposed requirements: favorable-biology unresectable liver disease with controlled primary, plus at least one trigger—refractory functioning syndrome, clinically meaningful liver-related functional compromise, or a prospectively documented credible threat to durable hepatic control despite reasonable alternatives. Do not require established irreversible failure before assessing benefit.

NET oncology and an independent transplant/HPB reviewer must agree that LT offers meaningful additional survival or symptom/function benefit over the patient’s accessible options, with B2 biological stability satisfied.

Asymptomatic stable low-burden disease with preserved hepatic function and reasonable durable options defaults to continued non-LT care/observation. Evaluate at least one appropriate treatment strategy; do not require two failures or exhaustion of every therapy. Do not use ENETS illustrative <30%/≥70% figures as a validated calculator.
questions.tests: Functional syndrome and treatment response; symptoms/liver reserve; growth trajectory; SSTR status and treatment alternatives; patient goals; independent benefit review.
questions.allocation: Favorable clinical prognosis does not establish urgency, exception entitlement or a reason to expose a healthy donor.
questions.rationale: Selected NET recipients can have excellent long-term survival, and comparative cohorts suggest potential benefit, especially over a decade. However, good post-LT survival is not synonymous with large incremental benefit: non-LT eligible patients can also live many years. The best Milan comparison adjusted delayed LT entry but remains confounded and predates most modern sequencing. The multicentre main-body matched OS difference is smaller than its abstract suggests. A credible benefit assessment must include both long-term hepatic threat and competing treatment/transplant harms.
questions.counter: Kjaer's eligibility-based non-LT cohort had substantial long-term survival; CLARINET supports prolonged control for indolent Ki-67 <10% disease. CABINET and PRRT offer additional disease-control options, but none is a randomized comparator to LT. Conversely, requiring every systemic option to fail may forfeit the transplant window and is not tested. Maspero documents late multisite recurrence and non-cancer deaths despite excellent LT survival.
questions.certainty: Low certainty for a causal LT benefit magnitude and any individual benefit cutoff; moderate certainty that NET biology and modern alternatives vary greatly. High-quality systemic-trial efficacy is indirect for transplant selection. No validated calculator supports the ENETS illustrative 30%/70% survival targets.
questions.threshold_basis: No randomized study validates a minimum survival-gain percentage, two-line failure count, or ENETS <30% versus ≥70% prediction. Six-month observation screens biology but does not prove added benefit. Any local two-reviewer requirement and reassessment cadence are governance, not biological cutoffs.

studies.population: Single-centre comparative Milan-NET study, 88 eligible patients: 42 LT and 46 non-LT, 1995–2010 era, nonrandomized. Well-differentiated portal-drained GEP primary, primary/extrahepatic disease removed, limited hepatic burden, at least six months stability; age <60 was relative. LT recipients were substantially younger (median 40.5 versus 55.5), and post hoc grading differed, including four G3 in non-LT versus none in LT. Primary regional nodes had been positive in 34/42 LT recipients; this is not evidence supporting active uncleared extrahepatic disease at LT.
studies.results: Median follow-up 122 months. Five-/ten-year OS 97.2%/88.8% LT versus 50.9%/22.4% non-LT. Time origin was primary-tumour resection; authors used left-truncated Cox models to account for delayed LT entry. Propensity-adjusted restricted mean survival gain was 6.82 months at five years and 38.43 months at ten years. These are cohort estimates, not individual calculators.
studies.limits: Major selection/age/treatment-era differences, small numbers and residual confounding remain despite statistical handling of delayed treatment. Only 4/46 non-LT patients received PRRT, so this is not a modern sequential-care comparator. Patients overlap subsequent Milan series and some multicentre LT studies; do not sum them as independent evidence.
studies.locator: Am J Transplant 2016;16:2892–2902; full PDF Methods statistical time origin/left truncation, Tables 1–2 eligibility/characteristics, survival and restricted-mean analyses.

studies.population: International retrospective comparison from 15 centres, 1988–2021: 455 patients (225 LT, 230 liver resection); median follow-up 97 months. Propensity matching produced 96 patients per group. Surgically selected patients, matched on age, grade and primary location. Twenty-seven percent of LT cases had unknown grade; burden, era and treatment history remain imperfectly controlled. Resection and LT do not necessarily address anatomically interchangeable patients.
studies.results: Use main Results p.e1067/Table 4: matched five-year OS 75% LT versus 68.3% LR, HR 0.56 (95% CI 0.35–0.90); five-year PFS 64.2% versus 14.2%, HR 0.25 (0.16–0.39), measured from operation. Ninety-day deaths 13/225 LT (5.8%) versus 3/230 LR (1.3%). LT G1 versus G2 five-year OS 92.9% versus 70%; adjusted G2 HR 2.52 (1.15–5.52). Outside-Milan matched OS HR 0.64 (0.31–1.33), not statistically conclusive.
studies.limits: Material abstract/body discrepancy: abstract reports matched five-year OS 73% versus 52.8%, whereas main Results/Table 4 report 75% versus 68.3%. The latter is used with explicit discrepancy flag; clarification would be desirable. Matching does not remove unmeasured confounding, missing pathology, era or selection bias. The nonsignificant outside-Milan estimate does not prove no benefit, and ten G3 cases do not validate G3 LT. Overlaps centre cohorts including Milan.
studies.locator: Ann Surg 2023 DOI10.1097/SLA.0000000000005663; PDF main Results printed p.e1067/Table 4 for matched outcomes; earlier Tables 1–3 for grade and mortality; abstract on first page differs.

studies.population: Retrospective Milan single-centre series, 1984–2019: 149 liver operations (53 LT, 96 LR), with 104 Milan-eligible cases analysed (48 LT, 56 LR). Portal-drained G1/G2 primary previously resected, no extrahepatic disease, <50% hepatic involvement, at least six months stable disease, age <60 relative. LT and resection had different resectability/age indications. Minimum six-month follow-up inclusion needs care when interpreting early risk; this is not an all-referral cohort.
studies.results: Time zero liver operation; median follow-up 158 months LT and 126 LR. Five-year OS 95.5% versus 90%; ten-year OS 93% versus 75%. Ten-year DFS 52% versus 18%; recurrence 25/48 versus 42/56 and median recurrence time 78 versus 24 months. LT recurrence was more often multisite; LR recurrence predominantly liver. Nine LT deaths included three cancer and six non-cancer deaths, including new malignancy, sepsis/lymphoproliferative and cardiovascular causes.
studies.limits: Not randomized or anatomically exchangeable; prolonged selected follow-up and differing age can favor LT. Strong overlap with 2016 Milan-NET makes it long-term/alternative-comparator information, not independent confirmation. Late recurrence and immunosuppression-related competing causes matter even with excellent survival.
studies.locator: Am J Transplant 2022 DOI10.1111/ajt.17156; complete PDF pp.2–4 methods/time origin/cohort; later survival figures, recurrence table and Discussion.

studies.population: Single-centre retrospective non-LT panNET cohort, 2000–2021: 519 screened, 41 G1/G2 metastatic patients included; 16 met at least one historical LT framework (Milan 11, ENETS 8, UNOS 13, overlapping). Resected primary, liver metastases, no extra-abdominal disease, age ≤75 and no G3. Definitions modified historical criteria, including Milan age <65 and two 'UNOS' patients with stable regional nodes, so not all meet today's NLRB requirements. Multimodal care included five liver resections, 15 ablations, six embolizations and later-line PRRT, not purely medical therapy.
studies.results: Time zero was date LT criteria fulfilled (for remaining patients, initial institutional visit after primary resection with liver metastases). Mean follow-up 5.4 years. Overall 41-patient median OS 9.3 years; five-year OS 64.7% (95% CI 48.2–81.2). Milan subset five-year OS 64.9% (32.2–97.6), ENETS 85.7% (59.8–100), historical UNOS 55.4% (26.0–84.8).
studies.limits: Small retrospective selected subgroups with very wide intervals; no internal LT comparator and treatment-era limitations. It challenges the assumption that eligible stage IV NET has uniformly poor non-LT survival; it cannot prove that non-LT is superior to LT. Avoid comparing its eligibility-based survival directly with post-LT curves as if randomized.
studies.locator: World J Surg 2023 DOI10.1007/s00268-022-06736-1; complete PDF pp.2–5 methods, time origin, eligibility modifications, treatments and survival tables.

studies.population: CABINET double-blind phase III randomized trial, 298 previously treated progressive well-differentiated NET patients: independent extrapancreatic cohort n=203 and pancreatic cohort n=95, 2:1 cabozantinib versus placebo. Prior PRRT and/or targeted therapy; advanced progressive disease, not specifically liver-only Milan-eligible transplant candidates. Different disease strata and prior-treatment burden preclude direct comparison with LT series.
studies.results: Time zero randomization. Median PFS 8.4 versus 3.9 months in extrapancreatic NET (HR 0.38, 95% CI 0.25–0.59), 13.8 versus 4.4 months in panNET (HR 0.23, 0.12–0.42). Objective response 5% and 19% in respective cabozantinib cohorts versus 0% placebo. Grade ≥3 adverse events approximately 62–65% versus 23–27%. The primary report does not establish an LT-comparable OS benefit.
studies.limits: High-quality evidence for this systemic-treatment setting, indirect for transplant benefit. A treatment's availability does not mean every candidate must receive it before LT, and its toxicities/tempo must enter individualized comparison. PFS is not OS and placebo control does not represent an entire modern lifetime sequence.
studies.locator: N Engl J Med 2025;392:653–665, online 2024; local complete PDF Methods, primary Results, response and safety tables.

studies.population: CLARINET randomized double-blind trial, 204 nonfunctioning advanced enteropancreatic NET patients (101 lanreotide, 103 placebo). SSTR-positive G1/G2 with Ki-67 <10%; 96% had stable disease over the prior 3–6 months; one-third had hepatic burden >25%. It represents indolent disease biology, not all progressive transplant candidates.
studies.results: From randomization, median PFS not reached with lanreotide versus 18 months placebo; HR 0.47 (95% CI 0.30–0.73). Twenty-four-month PFS 65.1% versus 33.0%. No significant OS or QoL difference in the primary report. Diarrhea 26% versus 9%.
studies.limits: Shows that stability and substantial survival without LT are plausible; does not estimate the added benefit of transplant or support treating all stable low-burden NET. G2 up to 20% and G3 are not represented by this <10% trial threshold.
studies.locator: N Engl J Med 2014;371:224–233; local complete PDF eligibility, Results and adverse-event table.

studies.population: NETTER-1 phase III randomized trial final OS follow-up: 360 assessed, 231 randomized (117 Lu-177-Dotatate, 114 high-dose octreotide), 223 treated in safety population. Progressive, well-differentiated G1/G2 SSTR-positive midgut NET on somatostatin analogue; not a liver-only transplant comparison. Corrected publisher version dated January 2022 reviewed.
studies.results: Time zero randomization; median follow-up about 76 months. Median OS 48.0 versus 36.3 months, HR 0.84 (95% CI 0.60–1.17), P=0.30; primary final OS endpoint not met. Forty-one of 114 controls (36%) crossed to PRRT. Two of 111 Lu-treated safety patients developed myelodysplastic syndrome, one fatal. Previously established PFS benefit and long-term tolerability remain relevant despite nonsignificant OS.
studies.limits: Crossover, additional therapies, attrition and distinct population prevent using median OS as a transplant counterfactual. Do not equate nonsignificant OS with no clinical activity, or assume PRRT has no long-term marrow risk.
studies.locator: Lancet Oncol 2021;22:1752–1763; local corrected PDF pp.5–6 participant flow/crossover/OS; safety Results and Discussion.

studies.population: ENETS 2026 position statement explicitly addressing controversies; expert, hypothesis-generating framework rather than original comparative outcome study. questions.proposal: Activate only well-differentiated G1/G2 disease from a known portal-drained GEP primary; retain a six-month biology test.
rules: Require expert pathology with Ki-67 <20% and the applicable mitotic criterion; use the highest reliable representative grade. Exactly 20%, rounding uncertainty or discordance is HOLD for adjudication, not rounding down. Do not impose an unsupported Ki-67 <10 rule or blanket G2 ban.

G3, NEC and unknown/nonportal primary have no active cohort in this edition. Extrahepatic disease, active or previously treated, follows NET-B4: resected nodes may qualify after clearance; previous solid-organ metastases do not.

Require ≥6 months of stable/responding hepatic disease and ≥6 months without recurrence after primary/extrahepatic clearance. Proposed documentation: at least three comparable assessments spanning baseline, about three months and six months. A suspicious new site is HOLD; confirmed progression restarts observation.
questions.tests: Expert grade/Ki-67/mitoses and primary origin; SSTR staging and cross-sectional imaging; complete primary/node/EHD clearance history; three-assessment timeline.
questions.allocation: Current NET guidance and clinical consensus differ on some boundaries; favorable guidance does not remove the need to prove B1 benefit.
questions.rationale: Evidence supports carefully selected well-differentiated G1/G2 portal-drained GEP primaries with cleared primary/extrahepatic disease and observed control. G2 has worse prognosis than G1 in the multicentre series but still meaningful selected survival, so a universal Ki-67 <10% rule would discard potentially suitable G2 without validation. Well-differentiated G3 and poorly differentiated NEC must be separated diagnostically, yet neither has an established LT-benefit pathway. Prior primary regional nodal positivity is not equivalent to active unresected extrahepatic disease.
questions.counter: Milan LT cohorts included many patients whose primary nodes had been positive, so 'ever node-positive means never LT' is too broad. However, retrospective final-pathology positive nodes do not negate the current cleared-disease requirement. Spanish OUT cases and the tiny G3 subgroup are too heterogeneous to validate expansion. NETTER-2 proves PRRT activity in selected G3, not LT efficacy after response; seven post-LT PRRT cases cannot guarantee safe salvage. ENETS controllable bone disease conflicts with NLRB's solid-organ exclusion.
questions.certainty: Low-to-moderate certainty for G1/G2 prognostic distinction and cautious standard selection; very low certainty for G3, nonportal/unknown primary, active nodes or prior solid-organ metastasis expansions. Official allocation exclusions should be reported separately from biological evidence.
questions.threshold_basis: Ki-67 <20% and six months after primary/extrahepatic clearance reflect current NLRB wording; modern WHO grading and the exact-20 boundary need explicit reconciliation. Six months stability derives from selection traditions, not a randomized timing trial. Three serial scans at roughly 0/3/6 months are a proposed local demonstration schedule, not a national mandated scan count.

studies.results: Time zero LT; median follow-up 6.5 years. Table 5: five-year OS 71.0% IN versus 58.7% OUT, ten-year 55.5% versus 32.0%, fifteen-year 52.2% versus 16.0% (OS comparison P=0.03). studies.population: European Liver Transplant Registry retrospective multicentre study, 213 recipients at 35 centres, 1982–2009; 107 before 2000 and 106 thereafter. Historical poor differentiation is not interchangeable with modern well-differentiated G3.
studies.results: Three-month mortality 10%. Five-year OS 52% measured from LT, versus 73% measured from liver-metastasis diagnosis; five-year DFS 30%. Post-2000 five-year OS 59%. Poor differentiation, hepatomegaly and concurrent major resection were adverse; age >45 was adverse in a later-era analysis.
studies.limits: The striking time-origin difference illustrates why survival curves cannot be compared casually. Registry era, incomplete grading and nonrandom selection limit modern applicability. Age 45 association does not establish a biological exclusion threshold. Cohort overlap with later multicentre reports is likely.
studies.locator: Ann Surg 2013 DOI10.1097/SLA.0b013e31828ee17c; PMID23532105 primary abstract; complete PDF not located.

studies.population: NETTER-2 open-label phase III randomized trial: 261 screened, 226 randomized, 151 Lu-177-Dotatate plus octreotide and 75 high-dose octreotide. Newly diagnosed advanced well-differentiated G2 Ki-67 10–20% and G3 >20–55%, SSTR-positive in all target lesions. G3 NET is biologically distinct from poorly differentiated NEC. This was not a trial of transplant eligibility or transplant bridging.
studies.results: Time zero randomization. Median PFS 22.8 versus 8.5 months, HR 0.276 (95% CI 0.182–0.418); objective response 43% versus 9.3%. OS was not mature. Safety populations 147 and 73: any grade ≥3 events 35% versus 27%, related grade ≥3 events 16% versus 4%; one myelodysplastic syndrome case and three grade-3 nephrotoxicity events in Lu-treated patients; no drug-related deaths reported.
studies.limits: Compelling systemic disease-control evidence for selected well-differentiated G2/G3, not evidence that responding G3 becomes suitable for LT or that marrow/renal injury is irrelevant to future transplantation. No NEC efficacy extrapolation. Full article reviewed now, upgrading prior abstract-only status.
studies.locator: Lancet 2024;403:2807–2817; complete PDF eligibility, efficacy, safety and Discussion.

studies.population: Retrospective seven-recipient case series of PRRT for recurrent NET after LT; abstract-only verification. Post-LT recurrence, not pretransplant bridging or a selection study.
studies.results: One partial response, five stable disease, one progression. Two grade-III myelosuppression events, one treatment cessation; proteinuria in four. No rejection reported over limited follow-up.
studies.limits: No control, tiny denominator and short follow-up; does not demonstrate durable salvage, long-term graft safety, or justify enrolling G3/extrahepatic cases because PRRT is available later.
studies.locator: Transplant Proc 2026;58:526–531; DOI10.1016/j.transproceed.2026.02.019, PMID41760506 abstract.

studies.population: Official Adult MELD Exceptions for Transplant Oncology guidance, December 2025 posting checked 24 October 2026. Allocation-review guidance, not national clinical policy or proof of efficacy. CRLM: BRAF wild type, microsatellite stable, R0 primary, at least 12 months from CRLM diagnosis and six months chemotherapy control; pretreatment largest lesion not >10 cm; no post-primary-resection extrahepatic disease, including nodes outside the primary field. Initial CEA exclusion is >80 ng/mL; extensions require <80. Lung/bone/other solid-organ metastasis history is a permanent exception-guidance exclusion.
studies.results: No efficacy denominator. NET guidance has no explicit numerical age or hepatic-volume cutoff. CRLM wording excludes >10% diameter growth or new lesions and labels this RECIST 1.1, although conventional RECIST 1.1 progression generally uses at least 20% summed-diameter increase plus an absolute change; record both, do not silently equate them.
studies.limits: Clinical judgment, exception endorsement and graft availability are distinct. A reasonable research hypothesis or living donor does not override allocation guidance or demonstrate acceptable benefit. At exactly CEA 80 the initial/extension wording differs; the draft's strict <80 harmonization is a conservative local rule.
studies.locator: Official PDF NET pp.8–9; CRLM pp.9–10; introduction on purpose/status.

studies.population: ENETS 2026 position statement explicitly addressing controversies; expert, hypothesis-generating framework rather than original comparative outcome study. Reorients toward incremental benefit and proposes substantial liver burden, young/fit patients and selected controllable extrahepatic disease; broadens beyond traditional Milan in some respects.
studies.results: No original outcome denominator. Proposed liver-burden bands around 25–70%, age <60 as relative and six-month stability are pragmatic concepts. Illustrative non-LT five-year survival <30% versus post-LT ≥70% are not a calibrated individual benefit model.
studies.limits: Do not turn an expert future-oriented proposal into validated numerical gates. Suggested controllable extrahepatic disease, including bone, conflicts with current NLRB solid-organ-metastasis exclusion. It identifies research needs rather than approving an expansion.
studies.locator: J Neuroendocrinol 2026;38:e70250; complete position-statement PDF burden, benefit, age, stability and extrahepatic discussion.

questions.title: Age and liver tumor burden
questions.question: Should age or burden remain local selection factors without being called national rules?
questions.status: Individual review · expansion not activated · not activated
questions.context: Age and liver replacement require individual benefit assessment; proposed expanded groups remain unactivated.

where.label: Request and renew the MELD exception

positions.says: “Metastatic diffusion to <50% of the total liver volume” A selection criterion in the Milan framework, not a national allocation ceiling.
positions.locator: Milan-NET, Table 1, PDF p2 / journal p2893

positions.says: “Age <60 years may be considered a relative, not absolute, factor.” Supports individualized benefit/fitness assessment rather than an automatic age exclusion.
positions.locator: 2026 full-text PDF p5, Table 2

questions.proposal: Use age as a review trigger, not an absolute exclusion; retain a conservative opening burden and a separately declared expansion band.
rules: Age ≥60 triggers explicit physiological-reserve, competing-mortality and benefit review; no absolute chronological-age ceiling or invented NET-specific frailty score is adopted.

Reproducibly estimate liver involvement. <50% is the conservative Milan-derived reference; exactly 50% through 70% is a separate prospective expansion stratum, not automatically active. >70% is outside the initial local program for conservative risk control, not because published evidence proves futility. The 50–70/>70 choices are local proposals, not national limits.
Low burden, particularly <25%, defaults to non-LT care unless a documented NET-B1 benefit trigger overrides that default. Do not give harmful downstaging solely to cross a percentage boundary.
questions.tests: Method/date of volumetric burden; functional reserve/frailty; competing illness; symptom/benefit trigger; current treatment alternatives.
questions.allocation: NLRB guidance has no explicit age or liver-percentage ceiling; identify these as local clinical/research choices.
questions.rationale: The <50% burden and relative age <60 framework has the best selected-cohort lineage, not proof of a sharp treatment-benefit boundary. Registry associations with age >45 or hepatomegaly do not establish universal bans. More burden may increase need for organ replacement but also worsen prognosis; low burden may predict good post-LT survival while yielding little extra benefit. NLRB's lack of explicit age/burden limits does not validate any expansion.
questions.counter: Spanish Milan-OUT survival is lower, but OUT combines many deviations and cannot isolate >50% burden or age ≥60. Matched outside-Milan confidence intervals are wide, not proof of futility. Kjaer's non-LT survival cautions against assuming any eligible patient needs LT. ENETS 25–70% proposal is an expert benefit-oriented hypothesis, not outcome-validated proof that 70% is a biological ceiling.
questions.certainty: Low certainty for any causal age/burden threshold; moderate confidence that these variables and liver function must be measured and followed. No prospective trial validates 25%, 50%, 70% or age 60 as a universal increment-benefit boundary.
questions.threshold_basis: <50% and age <60 relative originate in Milan selection; age >45 is historical prognostic association, not selection validation. ENETS 25–70% and six-month stability are pragmatic proposals. The V6 50–70% unopened stratum and >70% initial closure are local conservative design choices. Serial volumetry and trajectory matter more than a single imprecise percentage.

studies.population: Single-centre comparative Milan-NET study, 88 eligible patients: 42 LT and 46 non-LT, 1995–2010 era, nonrandomized. Well-differentiated portal-drained GEP primary, primary/extrahepatic disease removed, limited hepatic burden, at least six months stability; age <60 was relative. LT recipients were substantially younger (median 40.5 versus 55.5), and post hoc grading differed, including four G3 in non-LT versus none in LT. Primary regional nodes had been positive in 34/42 LT recipients; this is not evidence supporting active uncleared extrahepatic disease at LT.
studies.results: Median follow-up 122 months. Five-/ten-year OS 97.2%/88.8% LT versus 50.9%/22.4% non-LT. Time origin was primary-tumour resection; authors used left-truncated Cox models to account for delayed LT entry. Propensity-adjusted restricted mean survival gain was 6.82 months at five years and 38.43 months at ten years. These are cohort estimates, not individual calculators.
studies.limits: Major selection/age/treatment-era differences, small numbers and residual confounding remain despite statistical handling of delayed treatment. Only 4/46 non-LT patients received PRRT, so this is not a modern sequential-care comparator. Patients overlap subsequent Milan series and some multicentre LT studies; do not sum them as independent evidence.
studies.locator: Am J Transplant 2016;16:2892–2902; full PDF Methods statistical time origin/left truncation, Tables 1–2 eligibility/characteristics, survival and restricted-mean analyses.

studies.population: Retrospective Milan single-centre series, 1984–2019: 149 liver operations (53 LT, 96 LR), with 104 Milan-eligible cases analysed (48 LT, 56 LR). Portal-drained G1/G2 primary previously resected, no extrahepatic disease, <50% hepatic involvement, at least six months stable disease, age <60 relative. LT and resection had different resectability/age indications. Minimum six-month follow-up inclusion needs care when interpreting early risk; this is not an all-referral cohort.
studies.results: Time zero liver operation; median follow-up 158 months LT and 126 LR. Five-year OS 95.5% versus 90%; ten-year OS 93% versus 75%. Ten-year DFS 52% versus 18%; recurrence 25/48 versus 42/56 and median recurrence time 78 versus 24 months. LT recurrence was more often multisite; LR recurrence predominantly liver. Nine LT deaths included three cancer and six non-cancer deaths, including new malignancy, sepsis/lymphoproliferative and cardiovascular causes.
studies.limits: Not randomized or anatomically exchangeable; prolonged selected follow-up and differing age can favor LT. Strong overlap with 2016 Milan-NET makes it long-term/alternative-comparator information, not independent confirmation. Late recurrence and immunosuppression-related competing causes matter even with excellent survival.
studies.locator: Am J Transplant 2022 DOI10.1111/ajt.17156; complete PDF pp.2–4 methods/time origin/cohort; later survival figures, recurrence table and Discussion.

studies.population: International retrospective comparison from 15 centres, 1988–2021: 455 patients (225 LT, 230 liver resection); median follow-up 97 months. Propensity matching produced 96 patients per group. Surgically selected patients, matched on age, grade and primary location. Twenty-seven percent of LT cases had unknown grade; burden, era and treatment history remain imperfectly controlled. Resection and LT do not necessarily address anatomically interchangeable patients.
studies.results: Use main Results p.e1067/Table 4: matched five-year OS 75% LT versus 68.3% LR, HR 0.56 (95% CI 0.35–0.90); five-year PFS 64.2% versus 14.2%, HR 0.25 (0.16–0.39), measured from operation. Ninety-day deaths 13/225 LT (5.8%) versus 3/230 LR (1.3%). LT G1 versus G2 five-year OS 92.9% versus 70%; adjusted G2 HR 2.52 (1.15–5.52). Outside-Milan matched OS HR 0.64 (0.31–1.33), not statistically conclusive.
studies.limits: Material abstract/body discrepancy: abstract reports matched five-year OS 73% versus 52.8%, whereas main Results/Table 4 report 75% versus 68.3%. The latter is used with explicit discrepancy flag; clarification would be desirable. Matching does not remove unmeasured confounding, missing pathology, era or selection bias. The nonsignificant outside-Milan estimate does not prove no benefit, and ten G3 cases do not validate G3 LT. Overlaps centre cohorts including Milan.
studies.locator: Ann Surg 2023 DOI10.1097/SLA.0000000000005663; PDF main Results printed p.e1067/Table 4 for matched outcomes; earlier Tables 1–3 for grade and mortality; abstract on first page differs.

studies.population: Single-centre retrospective non-LT panNET cohort, 2000–2021: 519 screened, 41 G1/G2 metastatic patients included; 16 met at least one historical LT framework (Milan 11, ENETS 8, UNOS 13, overlapping). Resected primary, liver metastases, no extra-abdominal disease, age ≤75 and no G3. Definitions modified historical criteria, including Milan age <65 and two 'UNOS' patients with stable regional nodes, so not all meet today's NLRB requirements. Multimodal care included five liver resections, 15 ablations, six embolizations and later-line PRRT, not purely medical therapy.
studies.results: Time zero was date LT criteria fulfilled (for remaining patients, initial institutional visit after primary resection with liver metastases). Mean follow-up 5.4 years. Overall 41-patient median OS 9.3 years; five-year OS 64.7% (95% CI 48.2–81.2). Milan subset five-year OS 64.9% (32.2–97.6), ENETS 85.7% (59.8–100), historical UNOS 55.4% (26.0–84.8).
studies.limits: Small retrospective selected subgroups with very wide intervals; no internal LT comparator and treatment-era limitations. It challenges the assumption that eligible stage IV NET has uniformly poor non-LT survival; it cannot prove that non-LT is superior to LT. Avoid comparing its eligibility-based survival directly with post-LT curves as if randomized.
studies.locator: World J Surg 2023 DOI10.1007/s00268-022-06736-1; complete PDF pp.2–5 methods, time origin, eligibility modifications, treatments and survival tables.

studies.population: Spanish 13-centre retrospective series of 91 NET LT recipients, 1995–2024; 41 transplanted before 2007; 71 Milan-IN and 20 Milan-OUT. Mixed primary sites/eras and deviations. Pathology data missing in more than 30%; Ki-67 available in 51, with only one documented >20%. Milan-OUT combines different burden, primary, grade and other deviations; it is not a controlled trial of a single burden expansion.
studies.results: Time zero LT; median follow-up 6.5 years. Table 5: five-year OS 71.0% IN versus 58.7% OUT, ten-year 55.5% versus 32.0%, fifteen-year 52.2% versus 16.0% (OS comparison P=0.03). Five-year DFS 58.8% versus 36.3%, not statistically significant. Recurrence 52/91; ninety-day mortality 9/91 (9.9%). Nine retransplants: two primary nonfunction, six hepatic artery thrombosis, one rejection.
studies.limits: Era, missing pathology, small OUT group and composite deviations preclude validating 50–70% burden, age ≥60, G3 or extrahepatic expansion individually. Nonsignificant DFS is not equivalence. The abstract rounds OUT five-year OS differently; use Table 5 value with locator.
studies.locator: J Clin Med 2026;15:938; complete PDF Results, Tables 2–5, postoperative mortality/retransplantation and limitations.

studies.population: European Liver Transplant Registry retrospective multicentre study, 213 recipients at 35 centres, 1982–2009; 107 before 2000 and 106 thereafter. Published primary abstract reviewed. Heterogeneous historical NET pathology and selection; 55% had hepatomegaly. Major additional resection in 24 and minor in 30. Historical poor differentiation is not interchangeable with modern well-differentiated G3.
studies.results: Three-month mortality 10%. Five-year OS 52% measured from LT, versus 73% measured from liver-metastasis diagnosis; five-year DFS 30%. Post-2000 five-year OS 59%. Poor differentiation, hepatomegaly and concurrent major resection were adverse; age >45 was adverse in a later-era analysis.
studies.limits: The striking time-origin difference illustrates why survival curves cannot be compared casually. Registry era, incomplete grading and nonrandom selection limit modern applicability. Age 45 association does not establish a biological exclusion threshold. Cohort overlap with later multicentre reports is likely.
studies.locator: Ann Surg 2013 DOI10.1097/SLA.0b013e31828ee17c; PMID23532105 primary abstract; complete PDF not located.

studies.population: ENETS 2026 position statement explicitly addressing controversies; expert, hypothesis-generating framework rather than original comparative outcome study. Reorients toward incremental benefit and proposes substantial liver burden, young/fit patients and selected controllable extrahepatic disease; broadens beyond traditional Milan in some respects.
studies.results: No original outcome denominator. Proposed liver-burden bands around 25–70%, age <60 as relative and six-month stability are pragmatic concepts. Illustrative non-LT five-year survival <30% versus post-LT ≥70% are not a calibrated individual benefit model.
studies.limits: Do not turn an expert future-oriented proposal into validated numerical gates. Suggested controllable extrahepatic disease, including bone, conflicts with current NLRB solid-organ-metastasis exclusion. It identifies research needs rather than approving an expansion.

questions.title: Previously treated extrahepatic disease
questions.question: Which previously treated extrahepatic NET sites may enter the transplant route: resected regional nodes only, or also distant nodes and a solitary treated bone lesion as ENETS 2026 suggests?
questions.status: Resected nodes only, after clearance · not activated
questions.context: Use when the neuroendocrine tumor has involved sites outside the liver other than the primary (regional or distant nodes, mesentery, lung, bone or other organs), including disease later resected or treated with PRRT, ablation or radiotherapy.

where.label: Stage disease and confirm primary treatment

questions.proposal: Allow previously resected nodal disease after complete clearance and ≥6 months without recurrence. Keep previous lung, bone or other solid-organ metastases closed. Nodal disease cleared only by non-surgical treatment needs individual review.
rules: Previously resected regional or mesenteric nodal disease may qualify after complete clearance, as Milan-NET requires: the primary and all extrahepatic deposits removed in a separate curative operation, no recurrence for ≥6 months after that resection, and negative SSTR PET with CT/MRI repeated within 3 months of transplant consideration. Document stations, pathology and dates.

Nodal disease that resolved only after PRRT, ablation or radiotherapy is not equivalent to resection: individual review only, with SSTR-PET-negative status for ≥6 months. Persistent SSTR-avid or morphologically visible disease is active disease.

Previous lung, bone (including a solitary treated bone lesion) or other solid-organ metastasis remains closed, including after complete treatment. The ENETS 2026 position (no macroscopic, non-targetable extrahepatic disease) is recorded as a dissent, not adopted.

Extrahepatic progression during observation or on the waiting list removes the patient from the route; re-entry needs renewed clearance and a new ≥6-month recurrence-free interval. Plan hilar lymphadenectomy at transplantation, and clear extrahepatic disease in a staged operation rather than combining major extrahepatic resection with transplantation.
questions.tests: Operative and pathology reports for each extrahepatic resection, with node stations; SSTR PET (68Ga- or 64Cu-labelled) and CT/MRI within 3 months; date of the last extrahepatic treatment; PRRT cycles and response; serial imaging timeline.
questions.allocation: NLRB NET guidance requires resection of the primary and extrahepatic disease with no recurrence for at least six months, a negative metastatic workup including functional imaging, de-listing on extrahepatic progression, re-consideration only after extrahepatic disease has been zeroed for at least six months, and permanent exclusion for extrahepatic solid-organ metastases such as lung or bone.
questions.rationale: Milan-NET requires the primary to be removed with all extrahepatic deposits in a separate curative resection before transplant consideration, with restaging six months later; in the Milan cohort, 81% of recipients had node-positive primaries and 57% had positive hilar nodes, with 10-year survival 88.8%. Previously resected regional nodal disease is therefore part of Milan-NET, not an expansion. NLRB guidance encodes the same approach, de-lists on extrahepatic progression and allows re-consideration only after extrahepatic disease has been zeroed for six months. Functional imaging changes candidacy: 68Ga-DOTATOC PET removed 7 of 15 transplant candidates because of deposits not seen on CT or MRI.
questions.counter: Nodal involvement on final pathology was associated with worse survival after transplantation in the Milan cohort (HR 5.7, univariate), and first recurrences were mostly in distant nodes and bone, so a cleared nodal history is not risk-free. Concurrent resections at transplantation (mostly of the primary or other organs) were adverse in the European registry, borderline after 2000 (HR 1.9, p=0.058), and extensive concurrent primary or multivisceral surgery was adverse in a US series; both argue for staging the primary well before transplantation. ENETS 2026 proposes replacing “no extrahepatic disease” with “no macroscopic, non-targetable extrahepatic disease” (for example isolated resectable nodes or a solitary bone lesion amenable to local treatment); the authors present this as expert opinion, not outcome-validated. In small-intestine NET, any bone metastasis was independently adverse (HR 1.94) and 21% of patients with five or fewer bone metastases progressed beyond five.
questions.certainty: Low for accepting resected nodal disease after a recurrence-free interval; very low for PRRT-only clearance and for previous solid-organ metastases.
questions.threshold_basis: The six-month recurrence-free interval, functional imaging, de-listing on progression and the solid-organ exclusion are NLRB wording. Repeat SSTR imaging within three months of transplant consideration follows ENETS 2026. Treating PRRT-only clearance as individual review is a conservative local choice.

studies.population: Milan retrospective comparison: 48 transplant and 56 resection patients with NET liver metastases. Portal-drained G1/G2 primary previously resected, no extrahepatic disease, <50% liver involvement and at least six months of stable disease for transplantation.
studies.results: Node-positive primary in 19 of 24 transplanted patients with known nodal status (8 of 44 resected). Among recipients, nodal involvement on final pathology was associated with worse overall survival (HR 5.7, 95% CI 1.3–24). Recurrence after transplantation involved distant nodes in 16 of 25 and bone in 9 of 25.
studies.limits: Retrospective single centre; groups selected for different indications.
studies.locator: Am J Transplant 2022; Tables 1 and 3, univariate analysis.

studies.population: Milan prospective transplant versus non-transplant comparison (Milan-NET criteria). Primary removed with all extrahepatic deposits in a separate curative resection before transplant consideration; restaging six months after removal; at least six months of stable disease.
studies.results: Five- and ten-year overall survival 97.2% and 88.8% with transplantation versus 50.9% and 22.4% without; 81% of recipients had node-positive primaries and 57% positive hilar nodes.
studies.limits: Benefit shown only within Milan-NET selection; previous solid-organ metastases were not included.
studies.locator: Am J Transplant 2016; Tables 1–3 (full text).

studies.population: Official OPTN/NLRB guidance: Adult MELD Exceptions for Transplant Oncology. Resection of the primary and extrahepatic disease without recurrence for at least six months; negative metastatic workup including functional imaging; de-list on extrahepatic progression such as Ga-68-positive nodes; re-consider after extrahepatic disease is zeroed for at least six months; extrahepatic solid-organ metastases (lungs, bones) are a permanent exclusion.
studies.results: Allocation guidance; no outcome data.
studies.limits: Exception guidance, not an outcome-derived clinical rule.
studies.locator: Official PDF, NET section.

studies.population: 2026 ENETS position statement on transplantation for advanced small-intestinal and pancreatic NET. Replace “no EHD” with “no macroscopic, non-targetable EHD”; limited, completely resectable or otherwise controllable extrahepatic disease may not be an absolute contraindication; unresectable mesenteric nodal disease, certain bone metastases and brain metastases remain high-risk.
studies.results: No original outcome data; imaging should ideally be repeated within three months of transplant consideration.
studies.limits: Expert opinion, explicitly not outcome-validated; conflicts with the NLRB solid-organ exclusion.
studies.locator: J Neuroendocrinol 2026; updated selection principles.

studies.population: Single-centre imaging study: 52 NET patients comparing 68Ga-DOTATOC PET/CT with CT and/or MRI. Fifteen were evaluated for transplantation.
studies.results: PET/CT found additional hepatic or extrahepatic metastases in 22 of 33 with liver metastases and removed 7 of 15 transplant candidates (46.6%) from further screening.
studies.limits: Small; older tracer and era.
studies.locator: Ann Surg 2010; abstract.

studies.population: European Liver Transplant Registry: 213 transplants for NET. Twenty-four had major and 60 minor additional procedures at transplantation, including extended lymphadenectomy (38), removal of the primary (29), other organ resections (such as Whipple or exenteration) and peritonectomy.
studies.results: Major concurrent resection HR 3.1 across all eras; after 2000, any concurrent resection HR 1.9 (p=0.058); five-year overall survival 52% from transplantation.
studies.limits: Historical era; heterogeneous pathology.
studies.locator: Ann Surg 2013; Tables 4–6 (full text).

studies.population: Two Swedish centres; 138 small-intestine NET patients with bone metastases. Bone metastases on SSTR-PET; rarely biopsied; never curatively treated.
studies.results: Any bone metastasis HR 1.94; more than five lesions: median survival 18 vs 75 months; 21% with five or fewer progressed beyond five.
studies.limits: Small-intestine NET only.
studies.locator: J Neuroendocrinol 2025; Results, Table 5 (full text).

studies.population: Multicentre cohort, 28 centres (mostly US, also Canadian and European); 85 transplants for NET. “Extent of resection” meant concurrent primary or multivisceral surgery at transplantation, not clearance of metastases.
studies.results: Extensive concurrent surgery associated with worse survival (p=0.015).
studies.limits: No extrahepatic-disease variable; historical era.
studies.locator: J Surg Oncol 2015; Methods and Results (full text).

shared.title: Separate clinical, allocation, donor and study approval
shared.question: What are we approving?

positions.says: “This resource is not OPTN Policy” Guidance informs case review and is not itself binding policy or a clinical standard.
positions.locator: December 2025 oncology guidance p2, disclaimer

positions.says: “Function independently from the transplant candidate’s team.” Donor advocacy is independent of recipient-team enthusiasm.
positions.locator: Policy 14.2.A, PDF p285, living donor advocate requirements

shared.proposal: Require 100% completion of the applicable clinical, allocation, donor and research determinations before activation.
rules: Complete six separate dated determinations: clinical suitability; standardized-exception eligibility; nonstandard NLRB review status; calculated-MELD access; LDLT donor clearance; and research authorization. Mark nonapplicable domains explicitly with a reason—do not manufacture six approvals for every patient.
Any required missing, pending or adverse determination is a HOLD. An exception application is not approval, a donor is not recipient benefit, and clinical approval is not study activation.
Recheck the current policy/guidance version before each request; record actual decision and priority rather than predicted entitlement.
shared.tests: Signed suitability record; exact allocation route and policy version; exception outcome; donor-team status; study and institutional activation record.
shared.allocation: Policy 9.4 permits discretionary requests where appropriate; absence of favorable diagnosis-specific guidance is not absence of a review mechanism, and a request does not promise approval.
shared.rationale: The separation is a governance requirement, not an empirical survival cutoff. A clinically appropriate patient can lack exception eligibility, and an approved exception does not prove clinical benefit. LDLT requires an independent donor determination; a registry entry is not permission to perform experimental transplantation.
shared.counter: Not every case needs six separate affirmative approvals: several routes are alternatives or not applicable. An indiscriminate six-approval rule could obstruct appropriate standard care.
shared.certainty: High confidence in the separation of applicable authorities; no trial establishes that six boxes improve survival. Local workflow must map to current institutional obligations.
threshold_basis: Six domains: local checklist architecture, not six mandatory national approvals.
100% applicable completion: governance safeguard, not an outcome-derived percentage.
Hold pending required authorization: operational implementation of separate clinical, donor and research responsibilities.

studies.population: Binding OPTN policy posting effective 1 October 2026, checked 24 October 2026. Clinical candidacy, exception scoring, living-donor protection and reporting have different policy sections.
studies.results: Policy 9 governs liver allocation; Policy 14 requires independent donor advocacy/consent; Policy 18 specifies reporting. None establishes a universal cancer-benefit cutoff.
studies.limits: A center’s additional safeguards are not national policy. Review the active text and applicability before individual decisions.
studies.locator: Policies 9, 14.2–14.4 and 18; current official PDF.

studies.population: Current NLRB hepatic-adenoma guidance. Four alternative routes; route four contains conjunctive clinical requirements.
studies.results: GSD/Abernethy; OR unresectable β-catenin-mutated HCA; OR unresectable adenomatosis >10 lesions; OR unresectable, nonoperative-unresponsive and progressive/complicated HCA.
studies.limits: These are review routes, not proof of benefit or a mandatory transplant recommendation. Current text does not require all four conditions simultaneously or cirrhosis for all routes.
studies.locator: December 2025 oncology guidance, hepatic adenoma p11.

studies.population: Federal human-subject protection regulation. Applicability determined by institutional research/regulatory review.
studies.results: 46.111 requires risk minimization, reasonable risk–benefit, equitable selection, informed consent and appropriate monitoring. IRB approval is separate from OPTN allocation and clinical acceptance.
studies.limits: No prescribed ten-patient cap, five-patient interim or one-event statistical boundary; those require protocol-specific design and independent approval.
studies.locator: 45 CFR 46.111(a)(1–7), current official eCFR text checked 24 October 2026.

studies.population: OPTN Ethics Committee white paper, not a trial or binding allocation algorithm. Scarce-organ allocation must balance utility, justice and respect for persons.
studies.results: High predicted recipient survival alone is insufficient: opportunity cost, equity and access also matter. Donor autonomy does not remove clinical obligations.
studies.limits: Provides an ethical framework, not numeric weights, a universal survival threshold or permission to depart from allocation rules.
studies.locator: Introduction; utility/justice/respect-for-persons sections.

shared.title: Assess expected recipient benefit and organ use
shared.question: What is the relevant organ opportunity cost?

positions.says: “intention-to-treat population” The randomized pathway-level comparison is more informative than recipient survival alone; its selection and access conditions still matter.
positions.locator: Published TransMet report, primary analysis description

positions.says: “risks to donors remain incompletely characterized” LDLT transfers some risk to a healthy donor; it does not eliminate the need to establish recipient benefit.
positions.locator: 2026 published report, abstract background

shared.proposal: Require two independent recipient-benefit reviews and an explicit organ-use case; do not adopt a universal five-year survival cutoff.
rules: Proposed requirements: two reviewers not both responsible for recruitment must document expected incremental benefit over the actual contemporary alternative, with unresolved disagreement referred to the full committee.

For DDLT, show local expected access/dropout and sensitivity scenarios at 6, 12 and 18 months, total graft use including retransplantation, and plausible alternative recipients. These are planning scenarios, not imposed waiting periods.

For LDLT, separately show healthy-donor risk and potential downstream deceased-donor graft use. Do not call DCD, extended-criteria grafts or machine perfusion “zero opportunity cost.” No priority changes follow from an AI-selected survival threshold.
shared.tests: Same-eligibility/time-zero comparator; expected access; dropout; donor/graft type; uncertainty intervals; graft loss/retransplant estimate; written independent reviews.
shared.allocation: Only the applicable allocation process determines priority. Favorable post-LT prognosis, evidence grade and urgency are not interchangeable measures.
shared.rationale: Use pathway-level benefit from an agreed entry date, not recipient-only survival. Compare with contemporary tumor-specific care and actual local access. LDLT avoids one direct deceased-donor allocation but creates healthy-donor risk and may generate rescue graft use. Graft quality/perfusion changes do not make opportunity cost zero.
shared.counter: An ambitious prognosis threshold can exclude patients with substantial incremental benefit, while an indolent tumor can have excellent post-LT survival and little incremental benefit. Local wait times and unequal access can reverse a study’s apparent advantage.
shared.certainty: Benefit evidence differs by disease: randomized selected CRLM/HCC pathways cannot be generalized to all expanded indications. Ethical principles are authoritative frameworks, not empirically optimized allocation weights.
threshold_basis: Two reviewers: local independence safeguard, not validated optimum.
6/12/18 months: sensitivity scenarios for access/dropout, not mandatory waits.
HCC ≥60% five-year ITT OS: one expert trial-design benchmark; not a cross-cancer allocation policy.
All grafts: count initial and rescue/retransplant grafts; donor morbidity remains a separate outcome.

studies.results: From randomization, five-year overall survival was 77.5% with LT versus 31.2% without LT; tumor-event-free survival 76.8% versus 18.3%; median follow-up 71 months.
studies.limits: Strongest causal evidence for LT among selected responders, not for all 74 entrants or unlimited initial burden. Small, prematurely stopped trial. Appendix allowed uncertain bland-versus-neoplastic segmental/type-I portal thrombosis under additional response conditions; the actual PVTT denominator/outcomes are not reported. It must not be relabeled a proven-PVTT trial.
studies.locator: Complete accepted manuscript and protocol appendix; final published abstract for survival estimates. Avoid mixing accepted-manuscript and final-publication hazard ratios.

studies.population: Multicentre open-label randomized trial, 20 European centres, 157 screened and 94 randomized (47 LT-plus-chemotherapy, 47 chemotherapy); 63 screened excluded, including 13 with equivocal unresectability and 36 with progression. Age 18–65; ECOG 0–1; R0 colorectal primary; BRAF nonmutated; no prior or current extrahepatic disease/local recurrence; chemotherapy response or stable disease for at least 3 months, at most three lines. CEA <80 ng/mL OR at least 50% reduction from peak was permitted. Independent committee of at least two surgeons, two oncologists and one radiologist reviewed original and current lesion maps. These are trial criteria, not identical to current NLRB guidance.
studies.results: Primary time origin was randomization. Median follow-up 59.3 months. Five-year ITT OS was 56.6% versus 12.6% (HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.21–0.65); per-protocol OS 73.3% versus 9.3%. Of 47 assigned LT, 38 received LT and 36 were per-protocol; nine had progression-related exclusion/dropout. The control arm included seven subsequent resections and two LT crossovers. Safety population comprised 40 grafted patients. Among 36 per-protocol LT recipients, 26 recurred; 19/26 received chemotherapy and 12/26 local curative-intent treatment. Median per-protocol PFS was 17.4 versus 6.4 months, and secondary PFS after salvage was 35.4 months in the LT arm. Three of 36 per-protocol recipients required retransplantation (primary nonfunction, donor gallbladder cancer, caval obstruction/large-for-size); one postoperative death was reported. Serious adverse events occurred in 32/40 safety LT recipients. Median wait to LT was 50.5 days, which limits transfer to longer-wait systems.
studies.limits: Strong evidence for the selected trial population, not for BRAF-mutant, ECOG 2, active extrahepatic, truly NED, resectable or broadly expanded disease. PP survival conditions on reaching treatment and must not replace ITT. The Results recurrence denominator is 26/36; Figure 3 caption says 28 recurrences, consistent with a broader all-grafted report, so do not mix these denominators. QoL collection had only 55/74 per-protocol baseline questionnaires and is descriptive, not proof of a large QoL gain. Priority allocation and rapid access were part of the treatment strategy.
studies.locator: Lancet 2024;404:1107–1118. PDF pp.2–4 eligibility/committee; pp.5–6 trial flow/Table 1; pp.8–9 recurrence, safety, retransplantation, Figure 3; p.10 QoL/limitations.

studies.results: Simulation compared observed 2013 deaths/removals 93 (7%) and 4,581 patient-years with modeled TBS outcomes 48 (4%) and 5,262 patient-years. studies.limits: Simulated gains are not observed outcomes. Before/after implementation is nonrandomized and can reflect secular changes. Nonetheless it is meaningful evidence that a governed benefit-based system can be deployed, unlike a claim that all such models are unusable.

rules: Proposed readiness requirements: independent donor evaluation/advocacy, documented freedom to withdraw, recipient-benefit uncertainty consent, and funded medical, psychological, recovery and financial follow-up before investigational LDLT.

Proposed local follow-up: baseline, six weeks, six months, one year, two years, then annually through five years. Meet current OPTN reporting duties separately; this five-year support plan is not claimed to be a national reporting requirement.

One donor death, life-threatening complication, permanent major disability or liver failure requiring transplantation triggers an immediate pause of the relevant investigational LDLT activity and independent review. shared.allocation: LDLT clearance is separate from recipient selection; the potential need for retransplantation must be included in organ-use discussions.
shared.rationale: Donor mortality is low but not zero; complication, recovery and financial burdens are more frequent. Registry missingness and selected healthy donors limit reassurance. Five-year support is a reasonable local response to late morbidity, not a proven optimal schedule. Social vulnerability should trigger assistance, not categorical exclusion.
shared.certainty: Moderate certainty for the existence of material donor burden; lower certainty for individual risk and long-term recovery because of incomplete follow-up. No oncology-specific randomized donor-safety comparison.
threshold_basis: Baseline/6 weeks/6 months/1/2 years then annually to five: proposed support schedule; current mandatory reporting remains separately checked.
One sentinel event: conservative review/pause trigger, not a statistically estimated harm boundary.
No relaxed donor criteria: protection against shifting uncertain recipient benefit onto a healthy person.

shared.proposal: Use a small staged pilot with all-screened accounting and explicit safety pauses; no automatic expansion on favorable recipient survival.
rules: Proposed initial cap: ten transplants per separately approved biological stratum. Review after the first five have 90-day follow-up; no expansion decision until all first ten have at least 12-month follow-up. Reconcile vital status, graft events and known serious harms for every participant; require ≥90% completeness for other prespecified key outcomes.

In an initial experimental cohort, one all-cause recipient death, graft loss or retransplantation within 90 days triggers a pause of further experimental enrollment/transplantation pending independent review. A later possibly treatment-related death/graft loss or a donor sentinel event also triggers review/pause. Rescue care is never withheld; reopening requires independent authorization.

These are proposed conservative review triggers, not statistically validated efficacy/futility boundaries. Before opening, biostatistics and the independent board must ratify or replace them with indication-specific rules, denominators, pause authority and reopening criteria.

Capture every screened candidate, including nonrecipients, conversion to resection, dropout, deaths and access barriers; report survival from entry and from LT, recurrence, graft use, donor recovery and quality of life. Ten survivors alone do not establish benefit or authorize expansion.
shared.tests: Locked eligibility strata; prospective entry/time-zero dataset; modern comparator; adverse-event definitions; follow-up-completeness report; independently signed statistical and safety plan.
shared.allocation: Study monitoring never changes exception criteria or guarantees future access. Audit access by referral, geography, resources and donor availability without turning protected characteristics into exclusion rules.
shared.rationale: A small pilot can test feasibility, staging fidelity, data capture and acute safety, not prove durable survival benefit. Define time zero, all-screened enrollment, waitlist failures, post-LT survival/recurrence, competing death, all grafts, donor harms and patient-reported outcomes before opening. An independent board needs actual pause/reopening authority.
shared.counter: Zero observed events among ten fully followed independent patients still has a one-sided exact 95% binomial upper bound of 25.9% (1−0.05^(1/10)). Thus ten survivors cannot establish a <5% event risk. Ninety percent data completeness permits one missing patient; safety events and vital status require active ascertainment, not tolerance of unaccounted loss.
shared.certainty: Strong methodological rationale for predefinition and ITT accounting; no empirical validation of our exact cap/interim/completeness thresholds. Late recurrence demands multi-year follow-up.
threshold_basis: Ten per stratum and interim after five at 90 days: local feasibility cap and safety review cadence.

≥90%: proposed non-vital key-measure completeness threshold; not permission to ignore deaths/graft events or unknown status.
One early death/graft loss/re-LT: review/pause trigger, not automatic futility or withholding rescue.
